summary: Real-time Inter-network Defense (RID) helps service providers and security response teams communicate and trace security incidents such as worms, phishing, and denial of service. It defines extensions to IODEF for cooperative handling.

plainLanguage.summary: When someone is attacking networks, the networks' guards need to warn each other. This is a common way for them to send alerts and ask for help.

questions: how do isps share security incident info
what are the rid message types
how does a rid trace request work
subtitle: A common message format for service providers and response teams to ask each other to trace and stop attacks.

tldr.problem: When an attack crosses several networks, the teams that could trace or stop it have no standard, secure way to ask each other for help, and email may not be read with the needed urgency.
tldr.mechanism: RID wraps IODEF incident documents in a small XML envelope that names the message type, the destination and the sharing policy. Five message types (Request, Acknowledgement, Result, Report, Query) are signed, optionally encrypted, and passed between peers.
tldr.outcome: RID obsoletes RFC 6045, which moves to Historic status. This version is a Standards Track document, while RFC 6045 was Informational.

today: RFC 6545 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2012 that obsoletes RFC 6045, which it moves to Historic status. The unit metadata shows no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its transport is defined in RFC 6546.

sections.title: Why Incident Handlers Need RID
sections.content:
Real-time Inter-network Defense (RID) is a proactive way for service providers (SPs) and Computer Security Incident Response Teams (CSIRTs) to share incident-handling data. The RFC uses "SP" for any provider or CSIRT that takes part in RID communications. Incidents range from a benign configuration issue to a worm, phishing or a denial-of-service attack.

The hard case is an attack whose source is unknown, which needs to be traced step by step upstream through the network. The RFC notes that email may not be received in a timely fashion or acted on with the same urgency as a phone call or a mechanism like RID.

RID carries its data as XML, using the Incident Object Description Exchange Format (IODEF) from RFC 5070 plus RID-specific extensions. The RFC also says that sharing is not only a technical problem: procedural, trust and legal concerns may prevent sharing, so organizations apply their own policies on top of what RID provides.
sections.plainLanguage: If a bully keeps hitting kids on a long road, each house along the road needs a way to pass the word along. RID is the shared way to pass that word, so the grown-ups can find the bully and stop them.

sections.title: Consortiums and Communication Topologies
sections.content:
A consortium is a group of service providers or CSIRTs that agree to use RID under shared use and abuse policies. Peers coordinate contact details and the IP addresses of their RID systems, and a neutral third party may do incident handling for providers that lack the staff to do it themselves.

The RFC describes several ways to connect RID systems. In a direct peer topology two RID systems talk across an SP border. A consortium may follow its bilateral routing peerings, or build a mesh that gives a faster route to the closest upstream peer of an attack source. Broadcasting a request across a full mesh is possible but not advisable, because networks that never carried the attack traffic would spend resources on a needless trace. A star topology suits a peer that provides incident information to many consumers, such as a country-level CSIRT.

RID requests must be legitimate incidents and not used for sabotage or censorship, for example to rate-limit legitimate traffic so that papers cannot be read online.
sections.plainLanguage: Neighbors can agree to a phone tree. Some pass messages only to the house next door, some call across town directly, and a few share news with everybody who signed up. They also promise not to use the phone tree to be mean.

sections.title: The Five RID Message Types
sections.content:
RID defines five message types, and all of them MUST be implemented. They travel as an IODEF document together with a RID document, encapsulated for transport as set out in RFC 6546.

  • Request asks for help. With MsgType set to InvestigationRequest it alerts the SP closest to a source believed to be valid. With TraceRequest it traces traffic step by step when the source may be spoofed.
  • Acknowledgement tells the initiator the status of a Request, or why a Request, Report or Query was not accepted.
  • Result reports that a trace or investigation is done, whether a source was found and what was done.
  • Report files an incident with no action requested, for example for correlation or statistics.
  • Query asks a trusted RID system for information about an incident or incident type. The answer is a Report.

Compared with RFC 6045, this version merged the old TraceRequest and Investigation messages into one Request message, renamed RequestAuthorization to Acknowledgement and renamed IncidentQuery to Query.
sections.plainLanguage: There are five kinds of notes. One says "please help," one says "got it," one says "here is what we found," one says "FYI," and one asks "do you know about this?"

sections.title: The IODEF-RID Schema
sections.content:
RID is a separate XML schema, not an IODEF extension element. The RID message acts as an envelope: policy and security applied at the RID layer cover both the RID and IODEF documents. The RIDPolicy data also stays small and unencrypted, so a RID host can decide how to handle a message without decrypting and parsing the IODEF document.

The RID class has three optional parts and one required attribute, lang. Their roles are:

  • RIDPolicy, used by all message types, carries the message type (MsgType), the destination kind (MsgDestination), the Node to send to, an optional IncidentID, one or more PolicyRegion values and one or more TrafficType values.
  • RequestStatus is used only in Acknowledgement messages. Its AuthorizationStatus is Approved, Denied or Pending, with an optional Justification such as SystemResource, Authentication, Encryption or CannotProcess.
  • IncidentSource is used only in Result messages. SourceFound says whether a source was identified, and Node lists it.

MsgDestination is either RIDSystem (the next upstream RID system) or SourceOfIncident (the IP address of the incident source, used to find the RID system closest to it). PolicyRegion values such as ClientToSP, IntraConsortium, PeerToPeer and BetweenConsortiums show the expected sharing range, and TrafficType values such as Attack, Network and Content help a receiver decide whether to continue a trace.

The restriction attribute states how the sender expects the recipient to treat the data, but the RFC says it provides no real security because honoring it is the recipient's choice.
sections.plainLanguage: The RID part is the label on the outside of the envelope: what kind of note it is, who it is for and who may see it. The incident story sits inside, so the post office can sort the mail without opening it.

sections.title: How Exchanges Work
sections.content:
In an upstream trace, SP-1 sends a TraceRequest to its upstream neighbor SP-2. SP-2 replies with an Acknowledgement and, if it continues, forwards the request to SP-3. When a network locates the attack source, it sends a Result to the originator, using the path information carried in an IODEF EventData with category infrastructure. A Request involving several SPs relies on that path list. A RID system that sees its own information already in the path MUST stop the trace and should alert operations staff to a tracing loop.

If a request is denied, both the originator and the sending peer MUST receive the Acknowledgement, so the sending peer can try to stop or mitigate the traffic itself. A Pending status is generated automatically after a 2-minute timeout without approval or disapproval. For an InvestigationRequest the source is believed valid, so the request goes toward the network closest to it and the normal answer is a Result.

A Report needs no action beyond filing, and is optionally acknowledged. A Query is answered with a Report. The reply may preset a limit on how many incident documents it returns, with a recommended limit of 5, since other transfer methods may suit large transfers better.

A receiving SP MUST confirm that the traffic actually originated from the suspected system, and confirm the reason for the request, before it acts.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine passing a question down a line of neighbors until someone finds the culprit. Each neighbor says "I'm on it," and the one who finds the answer sends it all the way back to whoever started.

sections.title: Security Requirements
sections.content:
RID relies on TLS plus XML digital signatures and XML encryption, and the messages do not rely on the security of the transport alone. The RFC moves its normative security text into a dedicated Security Requirements section.

  • The originator of a Request MUST use a detached signature over at least one RecordItem, which is passed to all recipients. This lets each hop authenticate the original requester (multi-hop authentication).
  • For all message types, the full IODEF-RID document MUST be signed with an enveloped signature by the sending peer.
  • Content may be encrypted, as required by policy, agreements and data markers. Each participant MUST be able to do full path validation on the signing certificate.
  • RID systems MUST implement HTTPS as defined in RFC 6546, and MAY support others such as BEEP.

Trust is built on PKI. Entities compare certificate policies, and agreements SHOULD cover key management, path validation and Certificate Authority practices. The RFC also covers privacy guidance and sharing profiles that let organizations decide in advance what to share with clients, partners or consortiums.
sections.plainLanguage: Every note is signed like a letter with a seal that only the real sender can make. Important ones also go in a locked box, and every neighbor can check the seal before acting.

sections.title: Namespaces, Encoding and IANA
sections.content:
Every RID document MUST use the iodef-rid-2.0 namespace and start with an XML declaration, with UTF-8 encoding REQUIRED. RID and IODEF documents MUST be well-formed and validated against the schema, and DTD subsets are prohibited.

Other XML documents can ride in the ReportSchema element, provided the included schema defines its own namespace. A parser that meets an included document it does not understand MUST ignore it but process the rest, and implementations SHOULD NOT download schemas at runtime. IANA registers the namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:iodef-rid-2.0 and the schema urn:ietf:params:xml:schema:iodef-rid-2.0, and maintains the list of registered schemas allowed for inclusion.
sections.plainLanguage: The envelope must be written in one agreed alphabet and format, and it has a registered name so everyone knows which kind of RID note they hold.

items.label: Request
items.desc: Start or continue a trace toward the source.

items.label: Request
items.desc: Ask the SP closest to a believed-valid source to act.

items.label: Status
items.desc: Reports the status of a request, or why it was refused.

items.label: Outcome
items.desc: Says whether the source was found and what was done.

items.label: Report
items.desc: Files an incident, no action requested.

items.label: Query
items.desc: Asks a trusted RID system for incident information.
